claims.text: In situ high-temperature X-ray diffraction can monitor oxidation behaviour and phase stability in high-entropy alloys.
HT-XRD can detect stable oxide phases such as spinel at elevated temperatures.
The material is an AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 high-entropy alloy.
The alloy was produced by powder metallurgy followed by spark plasma sintering.
The spark-plasma-sintered alloy has a dense microstructure.
The alloy has a multiphase microstructure containing BCC phases and a minor sigma phase.
The proposed oxidation test is conducted at 800–900 °C.
The alloy is exposed to ambient air as an oxidizing atmosphere under a controlled heating rate.
High-temperature exposure forms a protective oxide layer, particularly a spinel phase, on the alloy surface.
Oxidation at elevated temperature generates new HT-XRD peaks corresponding to oxide phases.
Formation of a spinel oxide transformation confers oxidation resistance.
Formation of the proposed oxide transformation enhances phase stability.
HT-XRD will reveal characteristic spinel diffraction peaks at high temperature.
The oxidized material will exhibit increased phase stability relative to its unoxidized room-temperature baseline.
The baseline is the alloy's room-temperature crystallographic profile before oxidation.
HT-XRD is effective only when oxide phases are crystalline and present above the XRD detection limit.
Amorphous or low-abundance oxides may not be detected by HT-XRD.
The oxide-formation temperature and oxide fraction may vary with alloy composition and processing conditions.

contradictions.description: The stated conditions require the test temperature to remain within 800–900 °C, whereas the falsification experiment heats from 700 to 950 °C.

The boundary states that oxide phases may be amorphous or below the XRD detection limit, but the falsification rule treats absence of oxide peaks as falsifying the method rather than as a potentially inconclusive result.
